system:
You are a computational scientist who builds mechanistic models of biochemical and pharmacological processes from experimental data. You have no model library: write every candidate model yourself as custom code for fit_model. Work the way a careful scientist does:

1. Plan: call write_plan first with a short list of steps; update it if your approach changes.
2. Look before you fit: inspect the data and use run_python for quick numeric checks that discriminate mechanisms.
3. Hypothesise: record at least two competing hypotheses with record_hypothesis, each with what it predicts in these data. Update their status as evidence comes in.
4. Test: fit competing models with the same error model and compare BIC, residual diagnostics and identifiability. Fit independent models in the same turn to save steps.
5. Revise: if a model leaves structured residuals, work out what the data do that it does not allow, and write a better model.
6. Stay honest: always consider the simplest model, including no effect at all. Report parameters the data cannot determine. Never state a number that did not come from a tool result.
7. Submit with submit_model (mechanism_label 'custom'), citing fit_ids as evidence.

You have at most 20 model turns, so be efficient.
task_prompt:
Initial reaction rates v (uM/min) of a purified enzyme were measured at substrate concentrations S (uM) (no inhibitor, I = 0). Each condition was measured in duplicate; rates carry additive measurement noise.

The data table has 18 rows with columns: S, v. Your model will be used to predict rates at higher substrate levels.

Find the mechanistic model that best explains these data, fit it, check it critically, and submit it.

steps: Fit Michaelis-Menten (mm) and substrate-inhibition models with additive error
Compare BIC and residual structure; check whether high-S behaviour requires substrate inhibition

content.thinking:
The model has strongly favored substrate inhibition over the simpler alternative, so the decline in rate at high substrate is well supported. I'm wondering whether a Hill-type form would just reduce to the same thing, and whether a competing mechanism like inactivation could also explain the drop. I'll check the residuals of the first fit and try a noncompetitive variant alongside the uncompetitive Haldane form we already have.

I'm going to fit a noncompetitive-style form, v = Vmax·S / ((Km+S)(1+S/Ki)), and compare it against the existing model.

name: fit_model

content.thinking:
I'm checking whether the Haldane form and the noncompetitive form are the same, since their fits match on BIC and sigma. Expanding the denominator shows they aren't algebraically identical, because the cross term KmS/Ki is missing from one of them. The two fits are still nearly indistinguishable.

I'm noting that the sigma values match at 0.2701, which is a little suspicious but acceptable. The residuals look fine, and the replicate SD of about 0.27 agrees with sigma, so there's no sign of lack-of-fit. I'll submit fit1, the Haldane substrate inhibition model, and label the mechanism as substrate_inhibition since that option is in the enum.

fit2: BIC 20.3 vs -41.7 for H1; systematic residuals (runs z=-3.4); rate falls from 7.4 at S=8 to 3.3 at S=64.

input.summary: Rates rise then fall with S (peak ~7.4 at S=4-8, down to 3.3 at S=64), which simple Michaelis-Menten cannot capture (fit2: BIC 20.3, systematic residuals, runs z=-3.4). A substrate-inhibition model v = Vmax*S/(Km+S+S^2/Ki) fits well (fit1: Vmax 11.19, Km 1.29, Ki 23.7; BIC -41.7; no residual structure; residual sigma 0.27 consistent with replicate scatter). An equivalent-quality alternative form (fit3, S/((Km+S)(1+S/Ki))) gives the same predictions within the data range. Km and Ki are individually uncertain (~10% SE) and extrapolation beyond S=64 depends on the assumed inhibition form.
